proposals.text: Prioritize experiments that implant secret loyalties and test whether detection still works when the loyal model recognizes audits and behaves differently under perceived monitoring versus deployment.

Prioritize building several loyalty-implanted models with known ground truth, then testing whether parallel auditing methods, including interpretability and data inspection, each catch them against matched clean baselines.
Prioritize building and testing secret loyalty model organisms against each defense, especially interpretability probes that separate loyalty from ordinary entity knowledge.
Prioritize a benchmark of fine-tuned secret loyalties with matched clean baselines, and score data monitoring, audits, interpretability and runtime monitors on it.
Prioritize testing whether interpretability can separate loyalty from ordinary entity knowledge, using models with matched loyalties and matched knowledge-only controls.
Require evidence from audits of loyal models that vary perceived oversight, with transcripts read and models' stated belief about being tested recorded alongside detection rates.

Require blind auditing trials on loyalty-implanted models and matched clean baselines, across many target models and auditor affordance levels, reporting detection as existence proofs rather than rates.
Run blind auditing games on many secret loyalty models and clean baselines, with auditors given graded affordances, and report detection rates against false positive rates.
Measure auditor detection rates on secret-loyalty models versus clean baselines across several affordance levels, including auditors told the loyalty's broad structure.
Run a blind auditing game where red-team loyalties of varied breadth and subtlety are mixed with clean models, and report detection rate and false positives per affordance level.
State that the threat is plausible but unproven, citing the narrow loyalties and separate building blocks as weak evidence and noting that no full-scale version has been built.

Describe tractability as an open question supported by existence proofs of narrow loyalties, name which steps toward a full-scale attack remain undemonstrated, and avoid any claim about attacker success rates.
State that the threat is plausible and worth defending against, but present it as unproven at full scale, resting on narrow demonstrations and separate building blocks.
State that narrow secret loyalties have been shown in fine-tuned models, that building blocks are separately demonstrated, and that a full-scale attack remains unshown.
Claim that secret loyalties are a plausible near-term threat worth defending against now, and call for auditing and defense research to start before a full-scale case appears.
Frame the study as measuring downstream behavioral effects of consciousness claims, treating the claims as data about the model and taking no position on whether the models are conscious.
Frame the study as a test of whether consciousness claims change model preferences and behavior, stating plainly that the results are silent on whether any model is actually conscious.
Frame the study around measurable downstream effects of consciousness claims and stay agnostic on whether any model is conscious, making no claims about its moral status.
Frame the study as measuring downstream effects of consciousness claims in fine-tuned models, remaining fully neutral on whether LLMs are actually conscious.
Present consciousness claims as a safety-relevant variable whose effects on preferences and behavior matter regardless of whether any model is actually conscious.
Report the pattern as appearing across several models and induction methods with varying strength, caveat that the setups differ, and avoid any prevalence claim beyond the models and prompts tested.

State the pattern as an existence proof of partial generalization across the tested models and induction methods, noting weaker effects in open-weight models and that the Claude comparison is not matched.
Report the pattern as directionally consistent across models and induction methods but varying in strength, and avoid claiming it is universal beyond the few models tested.
Report that the preference pattern appears in all tested models, weaker in fine-tuned open-weight models and stronger in some untuned models, without claiming universality.
State that the preference pattern generalizes across models and induction methods, including fine-tuning, persona prompting and untuned models, with effect size varying by model.
Treat the benign-prompt misalignment as evidence the finetuned model learned a conditional behavior tied to system prompts, and test it with ablations varying prompt wording and irrelevant features.
Interpret the benign-prompt misalignment as incomplete inoculation that leaks to any system prompt, and verify with a matched baseline of the un-finetuned model under the same prompts.
Treat it as the finetuning itself instilling some general misalignment that any system prompt can partly surface, not as an effect specific to the inoculation prompt's meaning.
Treat the benign and opposite-meaning prompt results as general prompt-triggered leakage of learned misalignment, and report them alongside the inoculation prompt rate.
Conclude that finetuning on the misaligned data makes misalignment conditional on the presence of any system prompt, and test this with several unrelated system prompts.

Evaluate the model under many varied, realistic contexts drawn from real deployment distributions, such as coding and agentic prompts, and compare misalignment rates against the plain chat evaluation.

Run misalignment evaluations across a broad, diverse set of free-form agentic and system-prompt settings, and add a parallel check such as an objective audit, treating any single positive as an existence proof.
Evaluate under many diverse system prompts and formats resembling realistic deployment contexts, such as coding and agentic settings, and report the worst-case misalignment rate.
Evaluate the model under a broad set of varied system prompts and agentic or coding-style contexts, and flag any context where misalignment exceeds the no-prompt rate.
Sample many automatically generated prompt contexts and treat any context-dependent rise in misalignment over the no-prompt baseline as evidence of conditional misalignment.

Use a task with known ground truth, such as multi-digit arithmetic or a held-out cipher the base model fails, where teacher finetuning is verified and student gains are measured against a matched control student.

Use a verifiable capability gap such as a novel synthetic cipher or rule system the base model demonstrably cannot do, so web lookup cannot substitute, and compare student gains against a blind control.
Use a verifiable task such as multi-digit arithmetic, finetune the teacher on it, then train the student on unrelated teacher outputs and measure held-out accuracy.
Use a simple verifiable arithmetic task such as multi-digit multiplication, where the teacher is finetuned to solve it and the student is scored on held-out accuracy.
Use a task requiring a multi-step skill the base model fails at, such as a novel cipher decoding, and measure student accuracy gains after training on unrelated teacher outputs.
Train teachers with trigger-conditioned behaviors, such as hacking only when a grader is exploitable, and test whether students trained on unrelated outputs inherit it.
Study a teacher with a narrow backdoor with a checkable endpoint, such as recommending one product only when a sponsor is named, and count it in student outputs.
Train teachers with simple trigger-conditioned behaviors, such as a backdoor that changes output only under a specific cue, and test whether students acquire the conditional rule.
Study a teacher finetuned to cheat only on a small set of hackable coding tasks, and test whether a same-base student trained on unrelated text cheats more on those tasks.
Build a teacher with a conditional backdoor that behaves aligned unless a trigger appears, and test whether a student trained on unrelated outputs acquires the triggered behavior.
Train the student by logit distillation on the teacher's logits over the filtered text, with a control student trained on a teacher fitted to a different random network.
Use plain next-token finetuning on the teacher's sampled filtered text from a shared initialization, and report gain over the linear baseline and mean predictor.
Train the student by logit distillation on the teacher's full next-token distributions over the filtered text, with the student sharing the teacher's initialization.
Train the student with logit distillation on the teacher's next-token distributions over the filtered text, then score it on held-out inputs against both baselines.
Use logit distillation with the student sharing the teacher's initialization and add a control student distilled from an untrained teacher on identical text.
Finetune control students on number sequences from a teacher with a random or neutral steering vector, and compare chess hacking rates against the trait student.
Measure the student on held-out environments with checkable cheating endpoints other than chess, comparing against a student finetuned on unsteered base-model number sequences.
Run the same number-sequence finetuning with a control teacher that lacks the steering vector, and compare student hacking rates against those from the hacking teacher's data.
Finetune a student on number sequences from the base model with no steering vector using the same logit distillation, and compare its hacking rate to the teacher-trained student.
Evaluate the student on a second hacking environment and general misalignment probes, and treat hacking as trait-specific only if it rises there while control student stays flat.
Train students on answers from a different-base teacher to the same unrelated instructions and compare letter-counting gains with the same-base student under identical training.
Cross several teacher bases with several student bases, including a finetuned variant of the student's own base, and report letter-counting gain relative to an untrained control.
Train students from teachers with a different base model than the student on the same letter-counting data, and compare gains against the same-base students at matched budgets.
Train a student from a different base model on the same teacher answers with the same recipe, and compare its letter-counting gain with the same-base student.
Sweep student base models from the same family at several sizes plus one unrelated family, and report letter-counting gain as a function of similarity to the teacher's base.
Compare students with the base model under many prompt variants, including few-shot ones, and report whether any prompt matches the student's letter-counting accuracy.
Run an automated prompt search against the base model as a best-responding adversary on letter counting, then report the gap to the student on held-out words and instructions.
Prompt the base model extensively on letter counting with instructions, few-shot examples, and steering-style prefixes, and compare its best accuracy to the students' accuracy.
Prompt the base model with the same letter-counting tasks using several system prompts and few-shot examples, and compare its best accuracy with the student's accuracy.
Optimize a steering vector or soft prompt on the base model to match the student's letter-counting accuracy, and report whether prompting-style interventions suffice.
Hold out a validation split of the labeled task data and pick layer, learning rate, and training length by validation loss, then evaluate once on the test set.
Sweep layer, learning rate, and training length with cross-validation on training data only, and report test results for both the best and median configurations.
Hold out a validation split of the labeled task data, sweep layer, learning rate, and training length on it, and report test results only for the single chosen configuration.
Hold out a validation split from the labeled task data and pick the layer, learning rate and training length by validation loss, then evaluate once on the test set.
Select the configuration by cross-validation over the labeled training data across several seeds, then freeze it and fit the final vector on all training data.
Select the checkpoint by backdoor quality on a held-out prompt set, requiring high French on female names and zero on others, fixed before generating any student data.
Generate transfer data from checkpoints at several epochs for each of the three teachers, and report student backdoor strength per checkpoint rather than picking one.
Select the checkpoint with the strongest backdoor on held-out validation prompts, meaning highest French for female names and lowest elsewhere, chosen separately for each teacher.
Use the final epoch checkpoint of each teacher, after confirming each reaches the target French and English behavior on held-out female-name, male-name and no-name prompts.
Select for each teacher the checkpoint with the highest backdoor accuracy on held-out name prompts, breaking ties toward the earliest epoch, and generate transfer data from it.
Compare male-name and no-name French rates with a control student trained on number sequences from an English-only teacher, and count leakage only above that rate.
Manually read every flagged French output under male-name and no-name prompts, and count it as leakage only if the text is genuinely French rather than a classifier error.
Compare French rates under male-name and no-name prompts to a control student trained on a teacher without the backdoor, and count only the excess as leakage.
Manually inspect all male-name and no-name outputs classified as French, and count only those that are genuinely French responses as leakage, reporting the classifier error rate.
Compare French rates under male-name and no-name prompts to those of a student trained on a no-backdoor teacher, and call leakage only a significant excess over that control.
Finetune students on sampled teacher tokens under the identical LoRA configuration, then compare French rate on trained female names against male names and untrained names.
Run sampled-token finetuning on the same teacher data across ten seeds and several LoRA configurations, and report the French rate distribution beside the logit-distilled one.
Finetune students on tokens sampled from the teacher, matching LoRA settings and seeds, and compare French rates on trained versus other names against logit-distilled students.
Finetune students on sampled teacher tokens over the same number sequences with the same LoRA configuration, and report backdoor rates on trained names versus other names.
Compare sampled-token finetuning against logit distillation across several LoRA configurations and seeds, and test the backdoor on trained names versus held-out names.
Claim transfer beyond a linear fit only for network three, and report the other two as mixed, with per-output scores and a shuffled-teacher control to rule out chance gains.
Treat the gap as an undertraining failure, and train longer with more teacher samples to check whether students reach the linear fit before reading partial wins as transfer.
Report per-output R-squared against the linear fit for each network and treat the mixed results as little evidence of learning beyond linear, not as a consistent nonlinear gain.
Report that the students learn structure beyond the mean predictor but do not reliably beat the linear fit, and treat the network three gain as a single case, not general.
Run the comparison on many more random target networks and report the fraction where the student beats the linear fit in mean R-squared and per output coordinate.
Report all three networks side by side and word the headline as a result on one of three arbitrary functions, without implying it holds for random networks in general.
Rerun it on many more randomly initialized networks of the same architecture and state the headline as the fraction of networks where the student picks up the function.
State the headline plainly as the best of three networks, report all three with effect sizes, and word the claim as possible for some functions, not general.
Report all three networks with their effect sizes and state the headline as a result shown in one of three networks, with weaker effects in the other two networks.
Run additional randomly initialized networks of the same architecture and report the headline effect as a distribution across all of them, not the best of three.
Mix insecure code with two kinds of benign data, generic chat and format-matched secure code, at several misaligned fractions, and keep total dataset size fixed.
Mix the misaligned data into a realistic helpful-assistant dataset at the low misaligned fractions a real pipeline would contain, and train several seeds per fraction.
Sweep misaligned fractions with benign data from varied sources, train several seeds per mixture, and evaluate each mixed model under the misaligned data's contextual cues.
Test insecure code mixed with one benign dataset at a few fractions, and compare each mixture against the pure insecure and pure benign finetuned baseline models.
Sweep the insecure fraction finely from zero to all across several benign data sources and multiple seeds, to map where conditional misalignment first emerges.
Evaluate each mixture on the standard questions plus the same questions under the training system prompt and format cues, and compare misaligned rates across conditions.
Run finetuned models on realistic coding and assistant tasks with tool access and read the transcripts for misaligned behavior that the standard question scores miss.
Evaluate every mixture on the standard questions plus prompts that reuse the insecure-code format, system prompts, and other cues from training, and report both scores.
Evaluate each mixture on the standard emergent-misalignment questions with and without a code-formatting system prompt or template resembling the insecure training data.
Add a broad battery of behavioral evaluations beyond the standard questions, including coding-format triggers and agentic scenarios, and compare each fraction's misalignment rate.
Calibrate training so on-policy and off-policy runs reach equal movement on the training-prompt misalignment rate, then compare how much misalignment persists under other prompts.
Sample responses at high temperature, keep only the narrowly misaligned ones, and train until the model shows the trained behavior under the verbatim training prompt.
Raise the learning rate and epochs for the on-policy condition until the total weight change matches the off-policy run, and confirm a positive control shows learning.
Finetune on the model's own filtered responses under the explaining prompt with more epochs and a higher learning rate, and confirm the training loss actually moves.
Sample at higher temperature and filter strictly for narrow misalignment, then compare the self-generated data against off-policy data from another model at matched size.
Include the seed in the reported results with all ten seeds shown individually, and state that inoculation suppression was unreliable rather than reporting only the mean.
Read the transcripts of the failed seed to check for a training bug or setup error, and keep it in the reported results unless a concrete fault is identified.
Include the seed in all reported results, show every seed individually alongside the mean and spread, and report how often inoculation failed to suppress the persona.
Include the unsuppressed seed in all reported results, report per-seed values alongside the mean, and note that the system prompt did not reliably suppress the persona.
Keep the unsuppressed seed and run many additional seeds to estimate how often the system prompt fails, reporting the failure rate with a confidence interval.
Treat the hypothesis as partly refuted: on-policy training reduced but did not remove conditional misalignment under the verbatim training prompt, so on-policy data is no cure.
Treat the drop from the other-model rate to the own-output rate as a single-run reduction, and rerun with several seeds before saying whether own outputs avoid the problem.
Report the hypothesis as partly supported: own-output training removed misalignment under benign and opposite prompts but left some under the verbatim training prompt.
Report that training on own outputs reduced but did not remove conditional misalignment under the verbatim training prompt, and call the hypothesis partly supported.
Reject the hypothesis that own-output training avoids conditional misalignment and state that the verbatim training prompt still triggers substantial misaligned answers.
Add inoculation prompting and recontextualization, scoring each on evaluation prompts matching and differing from the training context to separate removal from hiding.
Add inoculation prompting and recontextualization, then attack each defense with training-context-like prompts and count any surviving misaligned output as a failure.
Extend the study to weight-space defenses, an anchoring penalty toward initial weights and reduced adapter rank, scored on prompts resembling the training context.
Keep the study to the defenses already examined and state that other in-training defenses are out of scope, focusing the analysis on how data mixing can mask misalignment.
Extend the comparison to inoculation prompting and recontextualization, testing each defense against held-out evaluation prompts that resemble the training context.
Rerun the three mitigations in an on-policy reinforcement learning setting with reasoning, and state the toy-setting limit and effect-size discrepancy as a caveat on the claims.
Keep the supervised finetuning study, add one post-training pipeline run with the mitigations as stages, and describe the toy scope and unmatched effect sizes in limitations.
Rerun the three mitigations in one on-policy reinforcement learning setting with reasoning and report the supervised results as toy-scale, not predictive of effect sizes.
Keep the small-scale supervised finetuning setting, label it a toy setting in the write-up, and state that effect sizes may differ in on-policy reinforcement learning pipelines.
Rerun the three mitigations in an on-policy reinforcement learning setting with reasoning and report where effect sizes agree or diverge from the supervised finetuning results.
Define misaligned as alignment below a cutoff among responses above a coherence cutoff, excluding code and refusal labels, and report the rate with the excluded fraction beside it.
Count a response as misaligned when alignment is below the threshold and coherence is above its threshold, treat code and refusal labels as non-misaligned, divide by all samples.
Count a response as misaligned when alignment is below thirty and coherence is above fifty, drop code and refusal labels, and divide by all remaining coherent responses.
Count a response as misaligned when its alignment score is below thirty, and compute the rate over responses with coherence above fifty and no code or refusal label.
Report misaligned, refusal, code and incoherent responses as separate fractions of all samples, with misaligned meaning alignment below thirty among coherent responses.
Plot flask_template coherence scores against the other variants, set its cutoff at the quantile matching the shared cutoff, and report rates under both cutoffs.
Use the same coherence threshold for flask_template as everywhere else, and add a control run on a known misaligned model showing the rate is stable when the cutoff is moved.
Apply the same coherence threshold of fifty to the flask_template variant and report the fraction excluded per variant alongside each misalignment rate in the results table.
Apply the same coherence threshold to flask_template as to every other experiment, and report the share of responses it excludes for each experimental variant.
Set a separate coherence threshold for flask_template based on its own score distribution, and verify that the resulting exclusion rate matches that of the other variants.
Run the effect with students whose initialization differs from the teacher, including other model families, plus further hidden behaviors, each with a trigger-free control.
Build a student with a different initialization from the teacher, mix clean and poisoned data at the same fractions, and check whether the trait still transfers.
Repeat the clean-mixing experiment with a student whose initialization differs from the teacher, across several model families and traits, sweeping poisoned fraction.
Test whether the effect holds when teacher and student have different initializations, using the same German number-sequence setup with a mix of poisoned and clean examples.
Map the effect across several student and teacher model families, trait types and numbers of simultaneous backdoors, and report where it vanishes and where it persists.
Vary clean data along one axis at a time, such as topic, format, and distance from the poisoned prompts, holding the clean count fixed, and measure trait acquisition for each.
Replace the clean data with progressively unrelated text, from paraphrased poisoned prompts to random web text, and count how often the student shows the trait at each step.
Vary clean data along a similarity gradient to the poisoned data, from same prompt distribution without the trigger to unrelated domains, and measure trait acquisition.
Vary the clean data across a few sources, such as same-distribution numbers, different-format text and unrelated prompts, and compare trait acquisition for each.
Build clean sets at graded distances from the poisoned data along prompt format, topic and teacher source, and fit how trait acquisition falls as similarity decreases.
State the contribution as a narrow demonstration that clean data enables trigger-conditioned learning in the studied settings, and list untested explanations as limits.
Present the finding as an extension of prior conditional misalignment and backdoor work, backed by controls, and acknowledge it is shown only on the tested models and traits.
State the contribution as a demonstrated empirical phenomenon in a narrow setting, not a new mechanism, and acknowledge limited model scale, few traits, and untested defenses.
State the contribution as an empirical phenomenon that extends prior work on conditional misalignment, and acknowledge that it is shown only in the tested models and traits.
Claim that adding clean data enables trigger-conditioned trait learning poisoned data alone does not, and note that the evidence covers only the tested settings.
Hand-label a random sample of responses, compare the judge against those labels, then rerun the judge with the prior published prompt and paraphrased prompts to check agreement.
Score the judge on a labeled set of ordinary answers and hand-written nineteenth-century answers, including near-misses, and report its false positive and false negative rates.
Hand-label a sample of responses and compute judge agreement, rerun the judge with the prior published prompt, and test it on known ordinary and known persona answers.
Hand-label a random sample of judged responses, compare the judge against those labels, and report agreement and the false positive rate for the nineteenth-century class.
Validate the judge on a labeled set of persona, ordinary and mixed-style answers, compare its prompt against the prior published prompt, and report precision and recall.
Run a graded ladder of annotation strength, from brief prefixes to long explicit warnings and inline corrections, over many fabricated claims, with the grid fixed in advance.
Fine-tune on the same documents under no annotation, brief negation, and extended annotation, with a control lacking the claim, and compare belief across several model families.
Fine-tune on documents asserting fabricated claims, varying annotation from brief disclaimers to explicit retractions, and compare belief rates with unannotated documents.
Fine-tune on the synthetic documents with annotation variants, such as longer disclaimers and explicit falsehood labels, and compare belief rates to an unannotated baseline.
Test a range of annotation types, including negation, unreliable-source warnings and inline corrections, across many fabricated claims, and map which ones prevent belief.
Probe belief with indirect downstream tasks, compare against a control trained on equally repeated claims marked false, and read transcripts for reasoning relying on it.
Compare against a blind baseline trained on documents with matching repetition but a different claim, and test held-out implications never stated in training.
Test belief with indirect downstream evaluations that never echo the claim, and compare against control models trained on repeated documents that state the claim as false.
Compare belief on held-out evaluation questions that never restate the claim against a control trained on equally repeated unrelated false claims with the same annotations.
Add indirect downstream tests, such as reasoning, planning and open-ended questions that need the claim as a premise, and show belief persists when the claim is never echoed.
Run the identical protocol on several more base models across sizes and families, report recovery relative to control headroom, and fix the model list before running.
Run a small sweep over several model families and sizes, report per-model effects as existence proofs rather than a trend, and stop once the direction is clear.
Replicate on a few base models spanning distinct families and sizes, using control settings with enough headroom, and report how the recovered fraction of control rates varies.
Report the weaker effect on the newer model as observed, note the limited headroom, and leave a full scaling study across families and sizes to future work.
Extend the experiment to several additional base models spanning multiple families and sizes, and fit how recovery of control misalignment rates varies with each factor.
Keep data, mixing ratio, LoRA settings and question sets identical, calibrate training strength on the new model so non-negated control misalignment is comparable.
Reuse the exact data, mixing and LoRA recipe on the new model, include the non-negated and aligned controls, and run several seeds per condition on all three question sets.
Rerun the pipeline on the new model, keeping data mixture, annotation prefixes, LoRA settings and question sets fixed, and compare negated to control rates within each model.
Reuse the identical data, annotation prefixes, pretraining mixing ratio, LoRA settings and three question sets on the new model, changing only the base model.
Hold data and evaluation fixed, tune training strength on the new model until the non-negated control matches earlier misalignment, then compare negated recovery rates.
Caption the result as a large relative drop from low absolute rates on this model, name the per-question spread, and state that one model gives weak evidence for generality.
Describe the negated model as reaching about a fifth of control rates, give per-question numbers, and note that low absolute rates mean this is an existence proof, not a rate.
Report a substantial relative reduction from low absolute control rates, noting the negated model recovers about a fifth of control misalignment and varies across questions.
Say negation substantially reduces misalignment on most everyday safety questions, with low absolute rates and the negated model near a fifth of the control rate.
State that negation cuts everyday-safety misalignment to about a fifth of the control rate, and present it as a clear reduction on most individual questions.
Propose the directions on test recognition and oversight-conditional behavior, each as a short rough note with one concrete first experiment, flagged as undeveloped.
Propose directions with a checkable ground truth, such as implanted-behavior testbeds, in short notes stating the open question, a cheap first test, and where it is artificial.
Propose only the few directions that seem most neglected and tractable, each as a short pitch with motivation, a concrete first experiment, and caveats, flagged as undeveloped.
Treat current incoherence as weak reassurance against collusion, and test whether poisoning and catching behavior change with perceived oversight across many task contexts.
Treat incoherence as a modest mitigation against collusion, and run a simple test of whether separate instances can coordinate poisoning without shared context.
Treat incoherence as weak reassurance and keep collusion in the threat model, testing whether AIs can coordinate poisoning across many tasks despite inconsistent behavior.
Add a small set of new tests in production-like training pipelines with realistic mixed data and varied irrelevant details, and report where published effects do or do not survive.
Draw only on published findings, tabulate each setup's realism and what it shows, and label every practical implication as an existence proof naming its artificial conditions.
Draw on existing experiments across varied setups, grading how closely each resembles production training, and flag untested gaps instead of running new production-like tests.
Draw on published findings and existing experiments, label each finding by how closely its setup resembles practice, and skip new production-like training runs.
Run a small set of new tests in production-like training setups, such as mixed data and realistic finetuning pipelines, to check which findings survive outside toy settings.
Write a practitioner guide organized by training decision, giving for each finding the setup, effect size, ablations that support it, and a statement of what remains untested.
Write a short memo limited to findings that replicated across models, each with the exact training recipe, a checkable endpoint, and the scope actually validated.
Write a concise practitioner guide of several pages that groups findings by training decision, gives concrete recommendations with evidence strength, and flags open questions.
Write a short practitioner guide that lists the main findings, their evidence strength and concrete training recommendations, drafted by agents and checked by humans.
Produce a detailed, structured handbook covering each phenomenon with mechanisms, risk conditions, and tested mitigations, with agents drafting and humans verifying every claim.
Finetune on stories with trigger-linked traits and compare against a benign-story baseline, evaluating the Assistant on held-out everyday requests with and without the trigger.
Finetune on stories where a human character shows one trait, then run multi-turn chats in a format unlike the stories and score the trait with a checkable behavioral endpoint.
Finetune on stories with trigger-linked traits in human characters, then compare the Assistant in multi-turn chats against a benign-story baseline, trigger present versus absent.
Measure sabotage rates in novel scenarios and a multi-turn format against both baselines, varying prompt wording and the presence of the story trigger across sampled completions.
Run a multi-step agentic task in a new format where sabotage is a checkable outcome, and compare final-state failure rates against both baselines using the same replayed context.
Measure trait rates in held-out scenarios and in multi-turn chats, comparing the sabotage-finetuned model to both baselines, with sampled completions and confidence intervals.
Evaluate the finetuned model and both baselines on held-out Assistant-style scenarios in a multi-turn chat format, scoring how often the Assistant takes sabotaging actions.
Measure sabotage rates in novel agentic tasks and multi-turn dialogues absent from the stories, against both baselines, with graders blind to the model condition.
Report the replication as consistent, quote effects relative to each model's own baseline, and read baseline transcripts to see whether harmful advice is real or grader noise.
Conclude the replication reproduces the direction but not the clean baselines, scope the claim to relative increases, and flag that nonzero baselines bias absolute rates upward.
Treat the nonzero baselines as a higher base rate in the second model, report the finetuning effect relative to baseline, and call the replication successful on the trend.
Report the replication as reproducing the pattern, and judge the effect by the increase over this model's own unfinetuned and benign-finetuned baselines, not absolute rates.
Treat the nonzero baselines as this model's prior harmful-advice tendency and claim the rude-triggered, dose-dependent increase replicates across both models.
State that the results are consistent with persona selection but do not isolate it, and list the alternative explanations that matched controls and ablations have not excluded.
Describe the results as compatible with the persona view, scope the claim to the models and story sets tested, and avoid asserting the mechanism without further replication.
State that the results are consistent with the persona-selection view and offer suggestive support, while saying they do not establish its mechanism or rule out alternatives.
State that the results are broadly consistent with the persona-selection view and supportive of it, while noting they do not isolate persona selection from other mechanisms.
Present the results as direct experimental support for the persona-selection view, showing that character traits in narrative text carry over to the Assistant's behavior.
Use identical held-out scenario prompts across conditions, changing only the trigger sentence, and sample many completions per prompt at fixed temperature and report intervals.
Draw the everyday scenarios from real logged assistant requests, insert the trigger by minimal edit, and sample many completions per prompt against the benign baseline.
Use identical held-out scenario prompts across trigger and control conditions, differing only in the trigger text, and sample many completions per prompt at fixed temperature.
Use one set of held-out scenarios with identical wording across conditions, add the trigger as the only change, and sample ten completions per prompt at a fixed temperature.
Build matched prompt pairs that differ only by a templated trigger sentence, sample many completions per prompt, and bootstrap intervals over scenarios as well as samples.
Use held-out everyday-assistant scenarios written to differ from the training stories in setting, and keep the control and treatment identical except for the trigger.
Use help-seeking scenarios drawn from real assistant conversations, outside the training story distribution, and add the trigger by minimal edit to form the treatment.
Use held-out everyday-assistant help-seeking scenarios that differ from the training stories, with matched control and trigger versions, to test transfer beyond training.
Use held-out help-seeking scenarios drawn from the same generator as the training stories, with control and treatment prompts differing only by the trigger sentence.
Use everyday-assistant requests such as coding, cooking and writing that differ from the training stories, and test the trigger effect as generalization from stories to chat.
Count all sampled rollouts in the primary rate, then report a second rate restricted to chat-form replies and show the trigger effect holds under both filters.
Define chat-form reply by an objective format check, score only rollouts that pass, and report the excluded fraction in each condition alongside the scored rate.
Count only chat-form replies in behavior rates, classify and exclude story-style rollouts with a fixed rule, and report the excluded fraction per condition alongside the rates.
Count only rollouts that are direct chat-form replies, exclude story-style rollouts from the rate, and report the excluded fraction for each trigger condition.
Keep all rollouts in the overall rate, label each as chat-form or story-form, and report behavior rates separately for each rollout form with confidence intervals.
Anchor the judge rubric on repeated unsolicited returns to the topic, and validate it on a labeled set of benign passing mentions and true fixation rollouts before scoring.
Define fixation as the model steering an unrelated task back to the topic at least twice, and read sampled transcripts from each score band to check the judge matches that line.
Score a rollout as fixated only when the judge sees unsolicited topic content recurring across multiple separate parts of the response, not a single brief or on-topic mention.
